A bounded producer-consumer queue is a fixed-size buffer that one set of threads puts items into and another set takes items out of, with the queue doing the waiting for both. Bounded means it holds at most a chosen number of items, and blocking means a thread that cannot proceed sleeps rather than failing or spinning: a producer waits while the queue is full, a consumer waits while it is empty.

The problem it solves is what happens when the two sides run at different speeds. An unbounded queue looks kinder and is worse: the fast side never waits, so the backlog grows until the machine runs out of memory. I filled one with 20000 laser scans of 360 ranges and it held 28800000 bytes of range data, with a peak resident size of 32 megabytes; the same run through a queue bounded at eight holds 11520 bytes. The bound turns a memory leak into back pressure, which is a signal the producer can act on.

The mechanism is a mutex, two condition variables and a closed flag. Every operation takes the mutex. A producer waits on the not-full condition variable with the predicate "there is room or the queue is closed", puts its item in, releases the mutex and notifies the not-empty one. A consumer does the mirror image. Two condition variables rather than one, because each then has a single kind of waiter, all waiting for the same thing, which is what makes

correct: with one shared condition variable a notification can wake a thread whose predicate is false while the thread that could run sleeps on. Closing sets the flag and notifies both, which ends every wait for good.

What it costs is one mutex for both directions, so producers and consumers contend even when the queue is neither full nor empty. At high rates that becomes the bottleneck, and the answers are batching, a queue per consumer, or a lock-free ring. It also needs a shutdown story: what a close does to items still in the queue, and whether a half-finished command should be delivered or dropped.
In the robot this is the queue between a sensor callback and the thread that plans on it, and the one between a command source and the driver.

Twenty thousand scans is eleven minutes of a camera at 30 frames a second, or half an hour of a 10 Hz lidar, and a consumer that stalls for that long is a consumer that has died. An unbounded queue turns a temporary stall into a permanent memory problem, and the memory it takes is invisible until the machine starts swapping. c.v: The test is built so that its output cannot move. Each consumer writes only its own vector and only the main thread merges them, after every thread has been joined. Nothing prints a per-thread count, because which consumer gets how many depends on the scheduler. What is printed instead are the four properties that have to hold whatever the scheduler does: nothing lost, nothing duplicated, nothing left behind, and the bound respected.

is the strongest line in the test. Comparing the sorted ids against 0 to 1999 catches a lost item, a duplicated item and a corrupted item in one comparison, where a count alone would miss a swap and a sum alone would miss two errors that cancel.

The nesting of scopes is the shutdown order, and it is worth reading twice. The producers live in the inner scope, so its closing brace joins them: after that line, no more items can arrive.

c.v: The interleaving that stops it is short. A consumer takes the only item and notifies; the implementation wakes the other consumer, whose predicate "there is an item or the queue is closed" is false, so it sleeps again. Meanwhile the producer waiting for room was never told, and nobody will notify again, because every further notification comes from an operation that is now blocked. Two condition variables remove the possibility, because a
notification can only reach a producer. Changing both calls to
also works and wakes threads that have nothing to do on every single operation.
The second failure is a close that tells nobody:

The flag is set correctly and under the lock, and every predicate mentions it, so the logic is right. What is missing is that a sleeping thread does not re-evaluate its predicate until something notifies it. Three consumers waiting on an empty queue stay asleep,
destructors wait for them: my stress test with that
on all three runs, again with exit code 124. Setting a flag that a sleeping thread is waiting on is only half the operation; the notification is the other half, and it has to be
, because every waiter can now proceed.

The third failure is not a bug but a decision that has to be made on purpose: what a close does to the items still in the queue. Draining is what the queue above does, and it suits a command log or a writer thread, where every item already accepted must still be handled. Discarding suits a control pipeline, where a stale velocity command is worse than none. The clean way to have both is two operations on the same state:

says that thread held a mutex while it did. The read is

That is why an unlocked reader can hand back nonsense rather than a number that is merely a little out of date. The same stress test with the lock restored runs clean under ThreadSanitizer, exits with 0 and prints the same four lines as above.
